title: Women's work in the past; interview consent and data sheet
description: Connie marvels at how much women accomplished without modern conveniences before asking Helena for permission to skip questions she finds too personal. She explains the biographical data sheet she will fill out, and Helena mentions a sister who traced the family tree back to England.

title: Helena's background; journey to Troy; parents
description: Helena spells her name and maiden name Cartwright, gives her 1899 birth date and Minnesota birthplace, and recounts arriving in Troy, Idaho on April Fool's Day 1912 by train with her parents and two sisters, carrying a kitten and a young hen called a pullet. They were hauled by lumber wagon through the mud to the farm, and she supplies her parents' names, dates, and occupations, her mother having been a teacher and her father a farmer.

title: Household pets; sisters' and husband's details
description: The conversation pauses for Helena's dogs and cats, including a yellow kitten rescued from a litter whose mother was poisoned. Helena gives her sisters Alva and Hesther's names, then details about her husband Edward, born in Minnesota in 1892 and married to her at home on November 27, 1926.

title: Edward's work; adopted son; Helena's education
description: Helena describes Edward's work as a logger and carpenter who built or remodeled many local houses, including additions to their own home. She tells of adopting their son Gerald, born in Spokane in 1931 and now a logger living nearby, then recounts graduating from Lewiston Normal School and taking special education courses at the University of Idaho that led to ten years teaching at the Opportunity School, though she never finished a degree.

title: Edward's stroke; communication and care
description: Helena explains that Edward suffered a stroke that took his speech and the use of his right arm, and for nine years he could not talk or write. She describes taking him to speech therapy in Pullman and how they communicated by pointing and guessing, as when he led her to the grocery store coffee counter, and notes he gradually regained reading recognition before he died.

title: Other jobs; wartime inspection work
description: Helena lists her other employment: telephone operator and, during World War Two, a federal pea and bean inspector at the warehouses, punching sacks and keeping sample records for pea and bean loads. She notes her education and teaching came before her marriage, and that she was commuting to teach in Troy and Deary when Edward had his stroke.

title: Hobbies; houseplants; honors and speech contests
description: Helena describes her hobby of clipping readings into scrapbooks for showers and religious occasions, coin and stamp collecting, and her many houseplants, including a blooming begonia and plants lost to frost in her makeshift greenhouse. She also tells of being PTA president and overcoming shyness to win bronze through diamond pins in WCTU speech and oratory contests.

title: Gaining confidence at school; early teaching; chipped tooth
description: Helena recounts feeling like the dull sister until she made the Science Club as an S-plus student on her own, which gave her confidence to teach country school with 24 pupils while attending summer sessions. She regrets missing her yearbook recognition after leaving school to fill a teaching vacancy, and tells of having a tooth chipped in a school clown-act boxing bout when a short classmate hit too soon and too hard.

title: Rural versus city life; farm childhood; chores
description: Helena explains her family's dislike of Spokane sidewalks and city restrictions and their eagerness to return to the farm, where children sledded, kept pets like the hen Becky and kitten Tommy, dammed streams, and played freely. She describes clearing the new farm of trees, picking up sticks for bonfires, and her father hauling loads on a stone boat pulled by a horse.

title: Farm settlement; water supply; childhood play
description: Helena Cartwright Carlson describes her father's purchase of the farm near Troy, Idaho, the process of clearing land for grain and hay, and the challenges of obtaining water through wells and hand pumps. She also recounts selling the farm and shares memories of playing with weeds, paper dolls, and a bent tree.

title: Pet squirrels; farm chores; schooling
description: She tells of adopting and taming squirrels as pets, nursing them through illness, and releasing one back to the wild when she left to teach. The conversation shifts to the difficult work of cultivating carrots for dairy cows, then describes walking to school, batching in town during high school, and the social divide between country and town students.

title: Modern childhood; grandchildren; household labor
description: She contrasts her unstructured farm childhood with modern children's scheduled activities. She discusses her grandchildren, including a granddaughter who left school early and divorced, and describes historical household tasks including carrying water, using outdoor toilets, and bathing in galvanized tubs.

title: Flour-sack clothing; straw ticks; smokehouse preservation
description: She describes making clothing from flour sacks, using straw-filled mattresses called ticks, and operating a smokehouse to preserve pork. She also discusses threshing crews and community meals.

title: Horses; food preservation; courtship and marriage
description: She complains about horse hair and odors from horse-drawn travel, describes ice boxes and baking from scratch, and expresses her preference for farm work over teaching. She concludes with how she met Edward Carlson while boarding at his sister's house and their courtship.
